# Sugarscape — 2D Agent-Based Social Simulation

A C++/OpenGL recreation of **Sugarscape**, the artificial society model introduced by Joshua Epstein and Robert Axtell in *Growing Artificial Societies: Social Science from the Bottom Up* (1996).

Agents live on a grid of cells that grow sugar (and, in one ruleset, spice). Each agent has its own vision, metabolism and lifespan. Nobody is told what to do — every agent follows the same small set of local rules, and the interesting behaviour (migration toward the peaks, wealth inequality, cultural blocs forming, tribal conflict along a border, trade between neighbours) falls out of those rules rather than being programmed in.

![Sugarscape running, with the console readout showing live statistics](docs/images/sugarscape-default.png)

The console window on the left is part of the program: it reports run status, speed, step count, and population averages that update every step.

## The Environment

The landscape is generated from user-supplied **sugar peaks**: an x/y coordinate and a radius each. Every cell measures its Euclidean distance to each peak and takes a maximum sugar capacity of 4, 3, 2, 1 or 0 depending on whether it falls inside 25%, 50%, 75% or 100% of that peak's radius. That is what produces the banded, terraced look of the terrain. Peaks may overlap, and their centres are allowed to sit off the grid, which is how the partial arcs in the screenshots are made.

In the trade ruleset, **spice fields** are laid over the same grid. A cell inside a spice field is flagged as a spice cell (its sugar is set to -1) and carries a flat capacity of 3 spice.

Agents are drawn as single points on top of their cell. Cell brightness indicates how much sugar (or spice) is currently on it; a cell that has just been harvested goes dark and regrows a unit per step.

Three colour schemes are included, switchable at runtime with the number keys:

## Architecture

The project is Model–View–Controller, with each layer talking to the others only through pure abstract interfaces (`modelInterface`, `viewInterface`, `controllerInterface`, `agentInterface`, `cellInterface`, `environmentInterface`, `ruleInterface`).

**Ownership is expressed in the pointer types, deliberately:**

- A cell owns its agent as a `std::unique_ptr<agentInterface>`. This makes it impossible for one agent to be held by two cells at once, and it means killing an agent is just letting the pointer go out of scope — there is no manual cleanup and no dangling reference.
- Moving an agent is a `std::move` out of the source cell into the destination cell, so the "an agent is in exactly one place" invariant is enforced by the type system rather than by convention.
- The controller owns the view and the model as `unique_ptr`s. The view and model hold a `std::weak_ptr` back to the controller, which breaks what would otherwise be a reference cycle.
- The environment is held as a `shared_ptr` so that weak references can be handed to rules without transferring ownership.

**Rules are objects** Every rule implements `ruleInterface::applyRule()`, which takes the cell array and mutates it. The model holds a `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<ruleInterface>>` and a step is simply each rule applied in order. Adding a new behaviour means writing one class and pushing it into the vector; changing the simulation's character means reordering the vector. Rule ordering is significant as moving before eating produces different dynamics from eating before moving.


## The rules

Every agent is created with randomised attributes: vision 1–6, sugar metabolism 1–4, spice metabolism 1–3, starting sugar 6–10, starting spice 10–20, maximum age 60–80, and a random binary gender.

### Movement

The agent scans outward along the four cardinal directions, up to its vision range. Unoccupied cells are ranked by current sugar; the best is taken, and ties are broken uniformly at random. If nothing better is visible, the agent stays put.

Agents are collected into a list and shuffled before moving, so no agent gets a systematic advantage from its position in the grid. The y axis wraps, making the world a cylinder rather than a flat plane.

This is the rule that produces the first recognisable Sugarscape result: agents rapidly abandon the flats and pile onto the peaks, and the population's average vision and metabolism drift as the badly-endowed agents die off.

### Growth

Every cell below its capacity regains one unit of sugar per step. Slow regrowth is what keeps the peaks valuable and the flats marginal.

### Consumption

An agent takes the entire sugar stock of the cell it is standing on and adds it to its personal store. The cell is left at zero.

### Death

Each agent's metabolism is deducted from its sugar store every step. Once the store goes negative, the agent dies and its cell is freed. This is why agents with high metabolism and low vision are steadily filtered out of the population.

### Ageing

Agents age one step at a time and die on reaching their maximum age. Combined with breeding, this gives the population turnover instead of a single cohort that dies out together.

### Breeding

An agent is fertile if it holds more than 12 sugar and is older than 15 steps. A fertile agent looks at its four neighbours for a fertile partner of the opposite gender, and needs an empty adjacent cell to place the child in. Both parents pay 12 sugar as the child's endowment, and the child is created in the empty cell with freshly randomised attributes. If the parent carries culture tags, the child inherits them.

The endowment cost is what keeps this from running away — reproduction is only possible for agents that have already succeeded at gathering, so the birth rate tracks the state of the landscape.

### Culture

Each agent carries a string of 7 binary culture tags, assigned randomly on the first step. On every subsequent step, each agent picks one tag position at random and flips that tag in each of its four neighbours to match its own value.

This is a tag-flipping contagion model. Left to run, it doesn't produce uniformity — it produces regions. Neighbourhoods converge internally and diverge from each other, and the boundaries between them move.

An agent's **group** is derived from its tags: if more than half the tags are 1, it belongs to group 1, otherwise group 2. Group membership is what the conflict rule acts on, and what the second and third colour schemes render.

### Conflict

Conflict replaces the standard movement rule rather than supplementing it. When an agent scans its vision range, it now also considers cells occupied by agents of the *opposing* group. Such a cell is a valid target if:

1. its sugar is at least as good as the best empty cell available, and
2. the occupying agent holds less sugar than the attacker.

If any valid targets exist the agent moves onto one, killing the occupant and taking a bonus of 2 sugar; otherwise it moves normally. Targets are shuffled before selection, and the whole agent list is shuffled first, so combat order is randomised.

The effect is a front line. Groups don't mix evenly — they press against each other along a boundary, and the weaker-endowed side gets pushed off the high-sugar terrain.

### Trade

The trade ruleset introduces spice as a second resource, with its own metabolism and its own store. An agent now needs both to survive.

**Trade movement** is need-driven rather than greed-driven. The agent computes its pressure for each resource as `stock / metabolism` and heads toward whichever resource it is shorter on. If nothing suitable is in range it moves to the edge of its vision to keep exploring rather than sitting still.

**The trade rule** itself works on abundance, using the same `stock / metabolism` measure. An agent with fewer than 5 steps' worth of both resources has nothing to spare and doesn't trade. Otherwise it is classified as sugar-rich or spice-rich, looks for an adjacent agent that is rich in the opposite resource, and the two swap everything they hold above five steps' worth. Both come away better hedged than they started.


---

## Rulesets

Chosen at startup. Rules run in the order listed.

| # | Name | Rules applied per step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Basic | Movement → Growth → Consumption |
| 1 | Standard *(recommended)* | Movement → Growth → Consumption → Breeding → Death → Ageing |
| 2 | Conflict and Culture | Movement → Culture → Conflict → Growth → Consumption → Breeding → Death → Ageing |
| 3 | Trade | Trade movement → Trade growth → Trade consumption → Trade → Death |

Ruleset 0 has no death or reproduction, so the population is fixed and you are watching pure foraging. Ruleset 1 is the classic configuration and the best starting point. Ruleset 2 layers cultural transmission and inter-group violence on top. Ruleset 3 swaps in the two-resource economy.

---

## Configuration

The program prompts for its parameters on the console before the window opens:

- **Grid size** — must be greater than 10. Recommended 51–200.
- **Number of agents** — must not exceed `grid size × grid size`. Recommended 400–4000.
- **Ruleset** — 0–3, as above.
- **Sugar peaks** — how many, then an x, y and radius for each. Coordinates may be negative or off-grid, and peaks may overlap.
- **Spice fields** — same format, requested only for the trade ruleset.

A run ends automatically after 500 steps.

## Controls

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `Space` | Pause / resume |
| `E` | Speed up (to a maximum of 4x) |
| `Q` | Slow down (to a minimum of 0.25x) |
| `W` `A` `S` `D` | Pan the camera |
| `1` `2` `3` | Switch colour scheme |
| `Esc` | Quit |

## Building and installing

The project is a Visual Studio 2022 solution (`408.sln`) and relies on VS to compile and link. Open the solution, then set up the four dependencies below.

Library and include paths are set by right-clicking **the project, not the solution**, and going to **Properties → VC++ Directories**.

### GLFW

Download the pre-compiled binaries from <https://www.glfw.org/download.html>, or build from source with CMake.

Once you have it, add the GLFW `include` folder to **VC++ Directories → Include Directories**, and the folder containing the built library to **VC++ Directories → Library Directories**.

### Linker input

Under **Linker → Input → Additional Dependencies**, add:

```
glfw3.lib
opengl32.lib
```

### GLAD

Generate a loader at <https://glad.dav1d.de/> with these settings:

- Language: **C/C++**
- Specification: **OpenGL**
- API gl: **latest version** (4.6)
- Profile: **Core**

Add the generated `glad.c` to the project, and link its `include` folder the same way as GLFW's.

### GLM

Download from <https://glm.g-truc.net/0.9.8/index.html> and add the root directory to the project's include paths.

### GoogleTest

Ships with Visual Studio 2022, so no separate installation is needed.

---

## Tests

Unit tests are written with GoogleTest and live in `test.cpp`, as a separate project inside the same solution. Because the model is built against interfaces rather than concrete classes, rules can be exercised against constructed cell arrays without standing up a window or a render loop.
